problems.title: One level of cache
problems.statement: A cache has a 1 ns hit time and a 5% miss rate. A miss costs 100 ns more.
hints: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.
problems.solution: $\text{AMAT} = 1 + 0.05 \times 100 = 6$ ns. The 5% of accesses that miss cost 5 ns on average, five times the hit time.

problems.title: Two levels
problems.statement: L1: 4-cycle hit, 95% hit rate. L2: 12-cycle hit, 80% hit rate among accesses that miss L1. DRAM: 250 cycles.

parts.prompt: What fraction of all accesses go to DRAM, in %?

hints: Nest it: AMAT = t₁ + (1 − h₁)(t₂ + (1 − h₂) t_DRAM).
The L2 hit rate here is local: it applies only to L1 misses.
problems.solution:
(a) $4 + 0.05\,(12 + 0.2 \times 250) = 4 + 0.05 \times 62 = 7.1$ cycles.

(b) $0.05 \times 0.2 = 1\%$ of accesses reach DRAM, yet they contribute $0.01 \times 250 = 2.5$ of the 7.1 cycles.

problems.title: Local and global miss rates
problems.statement: Measured over all memory accesses: 8% miss in L1, and 2% miss in both L1 and L2 (the global L2 miss rate). L1 hit 3 cycles, L2 hit 15 cycles, DRAM 300 cycles.

parts.prompt: The L2's local miss rate (misses / accesses that reached L2), in %?

hints: Local miss rate = global L2 miss rate / L1 miss rate.
Using global rates: AMAT = t₁ + m₁·t₂ + m_global·t_DRAM.
problems.solution:
(a) Only 8% of accesses reach L2, and 2% of all accesses miss there, so the local miss rate is $2/8 = 25\%$. A 25% local miss rate sounds terrible and a 2% global rate sounds great: they describe the same cache. Always say which one you mean.

(b) With global rates the nesting flattens: $3 + 0.08 \times 15 + 0.02 \times 300 = 3 + 1.2 + 6 = 10.2$ cycles.

problems.title: How good must the L1 be?
problems.statement: L1 hit 4 cycles; L2 hit 14 cycles with a local hit rate of 60%; DRAM 300 cycles. You need AMAT ≤ 8 cycles.
hints: Write AMAT as a function of h₁ and solve the inequality.
The miss penalty of L1 is 14 + 0.4 × 300 = 134 cycles.
problems.solution:
$4 + (1-h_1) \times 134 \le 8 \Rightarrow 1 - h_1 \le 4/134 = 0.02985$, so $h_1 \ge 97.01\%$.

Going from 95% to 97% hit rate is the difference between 10.7 and 8 cycles: in this regime every point of hit rate is worth a lot, which is why CPU designers fight for tiny improvements in L1.

problems.title: Stride and spatial locality
problems.statement: A loop reads 4-byte floats from a cold cache with 64-byte lines, at a fixed stride of s elements. Ignore prefetching.
hints: A line holds 16 floats. How many accesses land in each line?
problems.solution: A 64-byte line holds 16 floats. With stride $s$, consecutive accesses are $4s$ bytes apart, so a line serves $\max(1, 16/s)$ accesses and the miss rate is $\min(1, s/16)$: (a) $1/16 = 6.25\%$, (b) $8/16 = 50\%$, (c) 100%. Past a stride of one line, every access misses and most of each fetched line is wasted.

problems.title: Bytes fetched versus bytes used
problems.statement: You sum every 4th float of a 64 MB array that isn't in cache (64-byte lines).
hints: Floats 16 bytes apart: does any line go untouched?
problems.solution: (a) Every 4th float: a quarter of 64 MB, $16,777,216$ bytes. (b) Accesses are 16 bytes apart, so every 64-byte line is touched and the whole $67,108,864$ bytes come from DRAM. (c) 25%. On a GPU the same waste happens at 32-byte sector granularity, and it's the central topic of Part 2 (coalescing).

problems.title: Latency-bound or bandwidth-bound
problems.statement: (a) A program streams through 2 GB of data at a sustained 60 GB/s. (b) Another follows a linked list of 5 million nodes, each access missing to DRAM with 85 ns latency.
hints: (a) is limited by bandwidth: bytes / (bytes per second).
(b) has one access in flight at a time: count × latency.
problems.solution: (a) $2\,\text{GB} / 60\,\text{GB/s} = 33.33$ ms. (b) $5\times10^6 \times 85\,\text{ns} = 425$ ms. The second moves about 320 MB (5 M lines of 64 bytes), a sixth of the first's data, and takes 13× longer. Bandwidth-bound and latency-bound programs need completely different fixes.

problems.title: A loop with no overlap
problems.statement: A CPU loop does $10^8$ iterations. Each does one load and 2 cycles of arithmetic that depends on it, and nothing overlaps (no out-of-order, no prefetch). The memory hierarchy is the one from Problem 2 (AMAT 7.1 cycles). The clock is 4 GHz.

parts.prompt: Fraction of time spent waiting on memory, in %?

problems.solution: Cycles per iteration $= 2 + 7.1 = 9.1$, so $10^8 \times 9.1 / 4\times10^9 = 0.2275$ s, with $78\%$ of the time waiting. This is the single-thread picture that out-of-order execution and, on GPUs, multithreading attack.

problems.title: Working set of a matrix-vector product
problems.statement: Compute $y = Ax$ with $A$ a 4096 × 4096 FP32 matrix in row-major order, $x$ and $y$ FP32 vectors. The last-level cache is 4 MB, nothing is cached at the start, and every element of $A$ is used once.

parts.prompt: Minimum DRAM traffic in bytes, assuming x stays in cache once loaded?
Arithmetic intensity, in FLOPs per DRAM byte?

hints: x is 16 KB: does it fit in the cache alongside the streaming A?
FLOPs: one multiply and one add per element of A.
problems.solution:
(a) $A$ is $67,108,864$ bytes and must stream once; $x$ (16 KB) is read once and reused from cache for every row; $y$ is written once: $67,141,632$ bytes.

(b) $67,141,632 / 100\times10^9 = 671$ µs.

(c) $2 \times 4096^2 = 33,554,432$ FLOPs, so $0.4998$ FLOP/byte: one FLOP per 2 bytes. Matrix-vector products are hopelessly memory-bound on any machine, which is the root of Scenario 4 (LLM decode) much later.

problems.title: Caches don't save streaming code; concurrency does
problems.statement: One CPU core sums a 1 GB float array sequentially. Every line (64 bytes) comes from DRAM at 90 ns latency. Without a prefetcher, the core can have at most 10 misses outstanding.

parts.prompt: Time to sum the array, in ms?
With a prefetcher keeping 32 lines in flight, the new time in ms?
Would a cache twice as large help this loop?
options: Yes, the hit rate would double
No: every byte is used once, so there's no reuse to exploit

hints: Little's law, from Chapter 0.1: λ = bytes in flight / latency.
problems.solution: (a) $10 \times 64 / 90 = 7.11$ GB/s. (b) $10^9 / 7.11\times10^9 = 140.6$ ms. (c) $32 \times 64 / 90 = 22.76$ GB/s, so $43.9$ ms. (d) No: the array is far larger than any cache and each byte is used once. Prefetching helps because it adds requests in flight (Little's law); a bigger cache doesn't, because there is nothing to reuse.
